stories.headline: Paraguay's president impeached and jailed at home after a bank he favored collapsed
stories.what_happened: Santiago Peña, Paraguay's rightwing president, resigned and was then impeached by Congress after Ueno Bank, which had grown from an obscure digital lender to one claiming roughly 60% of the country's adult customers under his administration, was suspended over irregularities. The collapse left more than half of Paraguay's population unable to access their bank accounts, triggering protests. Minutes after being impeached, Peña was placed under house arrest and is now under investigation for allegedly using political influence to favor the bank's rapid expansion.
stories.potential_implications: This is the kind of story that looks, in retrospect, like an obvious bubble: a digital bank goes from nothing to 60% market penetration in a few years under a friendly government, and nobody asks too hard how. The pattern — rapid, politically-blessed expansion followed by a sudden freeze — rhymes with plenty of emerging-market banking crises, and the base rate for 'fast-growing bank with cozy government ties turns out fine' is not great. The immediate question for Paraguay is whether this stays a domestic political and liquidity crisis or spreads into a broader confidence run on the rest of the banking system; with 60% of the population locked out of their money, the pressure for a quick, credible resolution (deposit guarantees, central bank backstop, or both) is intense, and botching that risks turning a bank failure into a currency and investment crisis. For the region, expect increased scrutiny of fintech-style 'bank' expansions elsewhere that have grown unusually fast with unusually friendly regulators — this is a useful cautionary tale even without a direct causal link. The political angle is almost as interesting as the financial one: a sitting president impeached and put under house arrest within the same week is a fast institutional response by regional standards, which could reflect either unusually functional checks and balances or an elite consensus that Peña had become a liability worth cutting loose quickly to protect the system's credibility.

takes.text: frames the story primarily as a constitutional crisis, emphasizing the speed and formality of the impeachment and house arrest following millions of citizens being locked out of their accounts.
focuses on the financial mechanics behind the collapse, detailing how Ueno Bank's explosive growth under Peña's administration set up the conditions for the crisis.

stories.headline: Trump swaps chief of staff for immigration hardliner Stephen Miller, days after midterm drubbing
stories.what_happened: Trump announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of his administration's aggressive immigration crackdown, will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Wiles, the first woman to hold the post, is stepping down. The move comes just days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterms, a result widely read as voter backlash against the mass deportation campaign that put tanks and masked agents on residential streets. Democrats immediately criticized the pick, with some vowing to fight Miller's influence at every turn.
stories.potential_implications: The obvious reading is that Trump is doubling down rather than moderating after a clear electoral rebuke — elevating the person most associated with the policy voters just punished, rather than someone positioned to broaden the coalition. That's consistent with a pattern across his career: losses tend to produce more combativeness, not less. With Democrats now holding at least one chamber, a chief of staff chosen for loyalty and ideological purity over legislative dealmaking suggests the next two years lean toward confrontation — oversight fights, shutdown brinkmanship, maybe impeachment theater — rather than any pivot to compromise. The counter-case is that chief of staff picks are often more about internal White House management and message discipline than policy direction, and Miller's actual portfolio (deportations) may not expand much given legal and logistical constraints already in play. Worth watching whether enforcement activity actually intensifies in the next 60 days, or whether this is mostly a signal to the base that stays mostly symbolic.

takes.text: frames the appointment as Trump explicitly gearing up for confrontation with a newly empowered Congress, with Miller's combative reputation as the clearest signal of intent.
argues the pick shows Trump refusing to absorb the midterm message, accelerating exactly the policy voters just punished rather than retreating from it.
reports Democrats casting the appointment as a direct provocation, pledging to resist Miller's influence 'every step of the way.'

stories.headline: Europe hit by wave of coordinated hoax bomb threats against flights and broadcasters
stories.what_happened: Over the course of this week, more than 30 flights across Europe — affecting countries including France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia and the UK — received bomb threats, with another 18+ flights disrupted on Friday alone. No explosives have been found on any aircraft, and all affected planes landed safely. Media organisations in Ireland and the UK were also targeted with hoax threats, and a Russian extremist group has denied responsibility. Ireland's government described the pattern as "likely a coordinated campaign of disruption," and BBC Verify traced how one threat was relayed through air traffic control.
stories.potential_implications: The volume and spread — dozens of threats across nine-plus countries in under a week, hitting both aviation and media simultaneously — points away from copycat pranksters and toward something more deliberate, even if the "who" remains unconfirmed. European officials' instinct to call this hybrid warfare rather than random hoaxing fits a pattern seen with GPS jamming, undersea cable incidents, and arson plots over the past two years: low-cost, deniable harassment that costs the perpetrator almost nothing while forcing expensive responses (diversions, security sweeps, lost crew hours) on the target. The fact that a Russian extremist group denied involvement is itself informative — denial is cheap, and groups genuinely responsible for hybrid-warfare-style actions often do deny them, so this shouldn't be read as exculpatory. For travelers, the base rate of hoax threats actually containing a bomb is close to zero historically, so the practical risk to any individual flight stays low even as the aggregate disruption (delays, rebookings, media disruption) rises. The bigger thing to watch is whether European governments start treating this as grounds for retaliatory or defensive measures against a specific state actor — that's the threshold where a disruption story becomes a geopolitical one.

stories.headline: Iran war drags into its tenth month with strikes, satellite photos, and a tentative diplomatic off-ramp all happening at once
stories.what_happened: Trump said the US carried out another round of 'minor' strikes on Iran on Friday, hitting an air defense system near the Strait of Hormuz, days after an earlier attack became public. Satellite imagery reviewed by the BBC shows ongoing construction and digging near Iranian missile bases, suggesting reconstruction efforts despite months of US and Israeli bombing. Separately, Qatar is pushing a plan that would let UN inspectors visit Iran's bombed nuclear sites and potentially reopen the Strait of Hormuz, without requiring Iran to remove its enriched uranium stockpile. Ars Technica reports ships loitering near undersea cables amid Iranian threats to target that infrastructure if the US escalates further.
stories.potential_implications: The striking thing here is how little these four stories agree on where this is heading. You've got active strikes, active reconstruction of the targets being struck, active diplomacy, and an active threat to cut undersea cables — all in the same 72-hour window, which tells you the conflict has settled into something more like a managed equilibrium than a war with a clear trajectory. That's actually consistent with how a lot of these partial wars go: neither side wants full-scale escalation, but neither wants to be seen folding either, so you get periodic 'minor' strikes paired with backchannel diplomacy. The Qatari inspection plan is the more interesting signal for investors and shippers, since a credible path to reopening Hormuz would matter a lot for oil prices and insurance premiums on tanker traffic — but note Iran isn't being asked to give up the uranium itself, just to let inspectors look at it, which is a much lower bar than a real nonproliferation settlement and could unwind quickly. The subsea cable threat is the wildcard: it's cheap, hard to attribute cleanly, and would hit global internet and financial infrastructure far outside the regional theater, which is exactly the kind of asymmetric lever a weaker military power reaches for. If you're pricing geopolitical risk this week, the base rate says 'minor' strikes stay minor most of the time — but the combination of ongoing reconstruction and cable threats suggests both sides are also quietly preparing for the scenario where talks collapse.

takes.text: argues the satellite evidence of fresh construction near missile bases undercuts claims that strikes have meaningfully degraded Iran's capabilities, since Tehran appears to be rebuilding in real time.
frames the Qatari inspection proposal as the most concrete diplomatic opening in months, while noting Trump's threats of further strikes look less credible after JD Vance's recent remarks.

stories.headline: AI stocks sell off, then rebound, after Democrats' midterm sweep
stories.what_happened: Democrats took control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterms, and investors responded by dumping AI-linked tech stocks on fears that a divided government means tighter regulation and a slower AI buildout. Apple, Tesla and Nvidia together shed roughly $1tn in a single Thursday session, and the rout spread to Asia and Europe on Friday, with London at one point on pace for its worst day since March. By the following week, though, AI stocks had clawed back much of the loss. Separately, Elon Musk's $446m in PAC spending backing Republicans in five closely watched Senate races went for nothing — Democrats won all five.
stories.potential_implications: The quick round trip — trillions wiped out, then mostly recovered within days — is itself informative: it looks more like a liquidity-driven panic than a repricing based on new information about AI's actual prospects, since nothing about model capabilities or enterprise demand changed between Thursday and the following week. That said, panics and bubbles aren't mutually exclusive; a sharp, reflexive sell-off can also be the first tremor of something bigger, especially given how concentrated US index returns have become in a handful of AI-exposed names. Worth separating two different stories here: one is about AI valuations (stretched, by most conventional metrics, regardless of who's in Congress), and the other is about politics (a Democratic Congress genuinely does raise the odds of antitrust action, data-center scrutiny, or AI-specific rules, even with Trump still in the White House and able to veto most legislation). Divided government usually means gridlock rather than sweeping new regulation, which is probably the better base rate to anchor on. The more durable change may be reputational rather than regulatory: the tech barons who bet heavily on Trump, Musk most visibly, spent real political capital and got a rebuke from voters, which likely makes them more cautious operators for the next two years regardless of what bills actually pass.

takes.text: frames the rapid rebound as evidence the initial sell-off was more panic than a considered reassessment of AI's prospects.
is more cautious, noting this is at least the third tech-stock wobble this year over bubble fears and asking whether the volatility is a warning sign of a bigger meltdown still to come.

stories.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4%, warns of one more hike as Iran war feeds inflation
stories.what_happened: The Bank of England raised its base rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4%, the first increase in more than three years. Eight of nine Monetary Policy Committee members backed the quarter-point move; the ninth, Catherine Mann, wanted a larger half-point rise. The Bank's governor signaled another increase may be needed to counter inflationary pressure stemming from the Iran war, a call the Guardian notes cuts against the Office for Budget Responsibility's own forecast of falling inflation and tepid wage growth.
stories.potential_implications: The mechanical effects are well understood: variable-rate mortgage holders see payments jump almost immediately (the BBC profiles one borrower whose bill rose £200 a month), new fixed-rate deals get pricier, and savers finally get a slightly better return after years of near-zero yields. The more interesting question is what this rate rise reveals about the Bank's read on the economy. Raising rates during a second cost-of-living squeeze in four years is not something central bankers do lightly — it signals they see inflation risk from the Iran war as more durable than the OBR's models suggest, or that they're willing to tolerate short-term pain to avoid losing credibility on price stability. If the BBC's economics editor is right that one more hike is likely and then a pause, markets and borrowers should plan around a peak near 4.25%-4.5% rather than a sustained hiking cycle — but that forecast assumes oil-driven inflation from the conflict doesn't escalate further, which is exactly the kind of assumption that's failed repeatedly over the past few years.

takes.text: argues, via its economics editor, that one more rate rise is likely but that this hiking cycle should stop there.
frames the hike as politically jarring, noting it contradicts the OBR's own forecast of cooling inflation and weak wage growth, which will leave struggling households baffled by the timing.

stories.headline: Tesla winds down Cybertruck, bets Texas factory on robotaxis instead
stories.what_happened: Elon Musk said Tesla will stop building the Cybertruck at its Texas factory around the middle of next year, freeing up the plant to produce the Cybercab, Tesla's driverless taxi. The truck launched to enormous hype but sales fell almost immediately and never approached the volumes of competitors like the Ford F-150. Musk framed the move as a shift of focus toward autonomy and robotics rather than a retreat from passenger vehicles.
stories.potential_implications: This is less a story about one weird-looking truck than about where Tesla is placing its chips: away from selling individual cars and toward operating a fleet of self-driving ones, a bet that depends entirely on regulatory approval and self-driving tech actually working at scale, neither of which is guaranteed on Musk's timelines (his track record here is, generously, optimistic). The EV-market-share prediction market sits at 40% for 2030 and didn't move on this news, which makes sense — Cybertruck was always a tiny, idiosyncratic slice of EV volume, so its failure tells you much more about Tesla's product strategy than about electric vehicles broadly. Worth separating two possible readings: one, Tesla quietly admitting a flagship product flopped and dressing the retreat up as a pivot; two, a genuinely rational reallocation of a factory toward a higher-conviction bet once the truck had served its hype-generation purpose. Both are consistent with the facts, and the difference mostly matters for how much credit you give Musk's stated reasoning going forward.

takes.text: frames the announcement as Musk signaling a broader strategic pivot, with the Cybertruck's end simply clearing space for the Cybercab rather than being presented as a defeat.
calls it the end of a failed effort to grab a share of the lucrative US pickup market, noting Tesla never came close to challenging incumbents like Ford.

stories.headline: Binance's $6.3bn hack traced to a fake job interview, with North Korea the prime suspect
stories.what_happened: Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, disclosed that a $6.3bn hack was carried out after one of its engineers was approached through a legitimate job-hunting platform and lured into a series of bogus interviews with impersonated company representatives. The breach reportedly set off alarms across the crypto industry last Thursday evening. Investigators and reporting since have pointed to North Korea as the likely state actor behind the theft, continuing a pattern of crypto heists attributed to Pyongyang.
stories.potential_implications: If this follows the pattern of prior North Korea-linked hacks (the $625m Ronin Bridge theft in 2022, the $1.5bn Bybit hack earlier this year), the money likely gets laundered through mixers and shell exchanges before resurfacing to fund weapons programs — sanctions and cold-wallet freezes rarely claw back more than a sliver of it. The more interesting update is about attack surface: this wasn't a smart-contract bug or a private-key leak, it was a human being clicking into a fake interview. That's a cheaper, more scalable exploit than most DeFi vulnerabilities, and it means an exchange's security budget has to cover HR and recruiting pipelines as much as it covers code audits. Expect exchanges to start treating job applicants and recruiters as part of their threat model, which sounds absurd until you remember it just cost one of them $6.3bn. The bigger irony, worth sitting with: an industry built on the promise of removing trusted intermediaries just got taken for billions because one employee trusted the wrong intermediary.

takes.text: frames the breach as a straightforward case of social engineering, with Binance's own account emphasizing that a legitimate-looking job platform was weaponized to get a foot in the door.

situates the hack within North Korea's long-running crypto theft operations, asking what one of the poorest, most isolated states does with billions in stolen digital assets and why crypto's decentralization promise keeps failing to protect it.

articles.title: Kim Jong-un, crypto bros and a $6.3bn heist – podcast
articles.summary:
North Korea is said to be behind the theft from the crypto exchange Binance. How did they pull it off and what will they do with the money? Kalyeena Makortoff and Jean H Lee report

stories.headline: OpenAI's valuation jumps to $1.25 trillion as Anthropic edges toward an IPO
stories.what_happened: OpenAI closed a new funding round worth $11 billion, pushing its valuation to $1.25 trillion, according to Bloomberg. That's up sharply from the $852 billion valuation it carried after raising $122 billion in March. The news lands alongside reports that rival Anthropic is moving closer to its own IPO.
stories.potential_implications: A jump from $852 billion to $1.25 trillion in about eight months is a roughly 47% markup, which is either a sign that AI demand keeps outrunning even recent sky-high expectations, or a sign that private markets are pricing in a winner-take-most outcome before any revenue numbers justify it — probably some of both. Prediction markets currently put OpenAI's odds of IPOing before Anthropic at about 92%, with Anthropic's odds down a few points day-over-day to roughly 6%, suggesting traders see OpenAI's scale and brand lead as likely to translate into first-mover advantage in public markets too, even though Anthropic is reportedly further along in IPO preparations. If OpenAI does go public at anything near this valuation, it would immediately be one of the largest market-cap debuts in history, which raises the usual late-cycle question: are late-stage private investors handing retail investors the bag, or is this just what pricing power looks like when you're running the default AI product for hundreds of millions of people. Worth watching whether the next round, if there is one, comes at a similarly steep markup or whether growth starts catching up to valuation instead of the other way around.

takes.text: frames the valuation jump as part of a broader pattern of AI megadeals, noting it echoes similar reporting from the FT and Wall Street Journal about the same round.

stories.headline: Congress wants to talk to Jensen Huang about an alleged Chinese spy in Nvidia's orbit
stories.what_happened: The New York Times reported that China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang, an executive at AI firm Megaspeed, to gather intelligence on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and glean details about advanced American chip technology. The reported goal extended beyond simple espionage: operatives allegedly hoped she could help push Nvidia toward selling its most advanced chips into China. In response, members of Congress have summoned Jensen Huang to testify about his contacts and what, if anything, he knew.
stories.potential_implications: This lands at an awkward moment for Nvidia, which has spent two years threading the needle between its biggest growth market (China) and Washington's export-control regime, and which has no evident legal exposure here — Huang appears to be the target of the operation, not a participant in it. Still, congressional hearings have a way of generating their own momentum regardless of the underlying facts, and the optics of 'the most valuable chipmaker in the world was a target of PRC intelligence' will likely strengthen the hand of export-control hawks pushing for tighter restrictions on China-bound AI hardware, even though a tighter noose is precisely what Chinese intelligence agencies would want to avoid by instead trying to get access to current chips. One oddly placed data point: a prediction market asking whether Huang becomes the world's second trillionaire sits at 4% and didn't move on this news, suggesting traders don't see this story as materially denting Nvidia's business or Huang's personal position — for now the market is treating it as noise rather than signal. That could change fast if hearings surface anything suggesting actual company-level cooperation rather than attempted recruitment of an unwitting target.

takes.text: frames this primarily as a Washington story — lawmakers using the espionage allegations as a vehicle to press Huang publicly on Nvidia's broader China dealings, not just this one incident.

stories.headline: Dutch activists storm Microsoft datacenter site as Europe's AI backlash grows teeth
stories.what_happened: Members of the Dutch direct-action group Geef Tegengas broke into the construction site of a Microsoft datacenter in Amsterdam's Westpoort district, clashing with police, scaling a crane, lighting flares, and tying helium balloons to equipment. Separate demonstrations happened outside the site's fence, part of a wider wave of protests against AI infrastructure spreading across Europe. The actions target what organizers call the social and environmental costs of the AI buildout, including energy and water consumption.
stories.potential_implications: Datacenter protests have mostly been a NIMBY story in the US — fights over water rights in Georgia, grid strain in Virginia — but this is a more explicitly ideological, anti-AI-industry action, and it's notable that it's happening in the Netherlands, a country that already forced Microsoft and Google to relocate or scale back projects a few years ago after public pressure. One site occupation doesn't stop a hyperscaler; Microsoft will finish this building. But the pattern matters more than the incident: permitting delays, local referenda, and activist disruption are becoming a real tax on datacenter timelines in a way they weren't in 2023. Worth watching whether this pushes more capacity toward jurisdictions with less organized opposition, or toward supply arrangements that sidestep local grids entirely — which is part of why proposals for nuclear-powered datacenters on US military bases (prediction markets put the odds of the US starting that process by 2030 at 59%) look more attractive to operators than they did a year ago. Military bases come with federal land, existing security, and crucially, no city council to say no.

takes.text: frames the Amsterdam break-in as part of a broadening European backlash, with activists explicitly linking the AI boom's infrastructure footprint to social and environmental harms rather than treating it as a one-off local dispute.

situates the protest within a much larger and already bipartisan fight over datacenters' effects on power grids, utility bills, and nearby communities, suggesting Amsterdam is one data point in a global pattern rather than an isolated European phenomenon.

stories.headline: Chainalysis says hackers made off with credentials and tokens for its entire customer base
stories.what_happened: Chainalysis, the blockchain analytics firm widely used by law enforcement, governments, and crypto exchanges to trace illicit transactions, disclosed that attackers stole credentials and access tokens covering all of its customers. The company attributed the breach to what it called a "multifront cyberattack," saying the intrusion involved AI agents alongside an on-path (man-in-the-middle style) interception of data. Chainalysis has not yet detailed how the stolen credentials were used, how long attackers had access, or who is responsible.
stories.potential_implications: Chainalysis isn't just another SaaS vendor — its customer list skews toward people with a strong interest in not being watched while being watched: law enforcement agencies, regulators, and exchanges running active investigations into criminal wallets. If an attacker genuinely obtained working credentials for every customer, the realistic worst case isn't stolen passwords sitting in a dump somewhere, it's someone quietly seeing which addresses investigators are tracking, which tips off the people being investigated and can poison ongoing cases. The more mundane but still plausible case is that most of what was stolen were session tokens that get auto-revoked or expire quickly, in which case this is a bad week for Chainalysis's PR team rather than a live operational disaster. The detail worth watching is the AI agent involvement — not because it makes the attack scarier in itself, but because it's another data point in a pattern of attackers using agentic tooling for recon and lateral movement, which lowers the cost of this kind of multi-stage breach and means security teams should expect more of them, not fewer.

takes.text: frames the breach as unusually severe for a vendor whose customers include law enforcement and crypto firms, flagging the combination of AI agents and on-path data interception as evidence of an increasingly sophisticated, multi-pronged attack rather than a single exploited vulnerability.

stories.headline: HRV Pharma buys a German finished-formulations shop to get a foothold in Europe
stories.what_happened: HRV Pharma, until now mostly an active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) player, is acquiring 100% of Germany's Phatebo GmbH from ZeroStack. Phatebo makes finished drug formulations and supplies clinical trial materials, and reported revenue of roughly Rs 350 crore (~$42 million) in 2025. The deal gives HRV its first finished-formulations business plus a licensed pharmaceutical operating entity inside the EU. No purchase price was disclosed in any of the coverage.
stories.potential_implications: This is a fairly standard move in the Indian pharma playbook: buy a small, already-licensed European operator rather than spend years navigating EU GMP approval and market-access rules from scratch. The prize isn't really Phatebo's revenue (modest by industry standards) — it's the regulatory license and the clinical-trial-supply niche, which is a decent hedge against tariff and supply-chain disruptions that have made Western buyers nervous about depending on India-only manufacturing. Worth watching whether this is a one-off or the start of a pattern — if more mid-size Indian API/generics players start snapping up small EU formulation and clinical-supply businesses over the next year, that's a signal the roll-up logic (acquire license + capability, keep cost base in India) is becoming the default strategy rather than the exception. The flip side: without disclosed deal terms, it's hard to know if HRV overpaid for the license or got a bargain, and a business this size won't move HRV's overall trajectory much on its own.

takes.text: frames this mainly as HRV's strategic pivot beyond commodity APIs into higher-value finished formulations, with the German licensed entity as the key asset gained.
emphasizes the clinical-trial-supply angle, positioning the deal as HRV buying its way into a specialized, less commoditized corner of pharma services.

highlights the hard numbers — a full 100% buyout from ZeroStack and Phatebo's Rs 350 crore 2025 revenue — framing the acquisition as HRV's entry ticket into European markets broadly, not just a single product line.

stories.headline: A diet-heart study finds a subtle signal, and plenty of reasons to shrug
stories.what_happened: Researchers analyzed data from 7,256 adults in the Maastricht Study, a Dutch population cohort, looking for links between diet quality and heart rate variability (HRV), a marker of autonomic nervous system function. People who more closely followed the DASH diet or the Dutch Healthy Diet pattern showed higher very-low-frequency (VLF) HRV power, an effect concentrated among those not taking beta-blockers. After full statistical adjustment, the more commonly cited time-domain HRV measures showed no significant association with diet at all.
stories.potential_implications: This is a cross-sectional snapshot, not a trial, so the honest reading is correlation with a side order of maybe-causation. VLF HRV itself is a somewhat obscure and contested metric — researchers still argue about what physiological process it actually tracks, which makes it a shakier foundation for health claims than, say, LDL cholesterol or blood pressure. The fact that the more standard time-domain HRV measures showed nothing after adjustment is the kind of result that should make you discount the headline finding rather than inflate it; in observational nutrition science, a pattern that only shows up in one of several measured outcomes is more often noise than signal, especially once you account for how many comparisons got run to find it. None of this means DASH or Dutch-style eating patterns are bad for you — the existing evidence on DASH and cardiovascular risk is reasonably solid from other angles — but this particular study adds a thin, hedged data point rather than a load-bearing one. The beta-blocker interaction is an interesting thread (drugs that blunt autonomic signaling would plausibly mask diet-driven HRV effects), but it's also exactly the kind of subgroup finding that looks compelling until someone tries to replicate it.

takes.text: frames the result cautiously, emphasizing that the association appeared only in one HRV measure and stopping well short of claiming the diets improve cardiovascular function.

articles.title: Two healthy diets stood out in a study of more than 7,000 adults
articles.summary: In a cross-sectional analysis of 7,256 adults from the Maastricht Study, researchers found that greater adherence to the DASH and Dutch Healthy Diet patterns was associated with higher very-low-frequency (VLF) heart rate variability power, particularly among participants not taking beta-blockers. No significant associations were observed across time-domain HRV measures after full adjustment, and the findings do not establish that these diets improve cardiovascular function.

human_story.headline: The 12-Day Search to Return a Stranger's Salary
human_story.text: In a public plaza in southern Brazil, Pedro Moro spotted a wad of cash lying on the ground with no one in sight to claim it. He soon realized it wasn't pocket change — it was an entire month's wages that a young construction laborer had just withdrawn from the bank, money meant for his daughter. Rather than keep it or hand it to the police and move on, Moro spent the next 12 days tracking down the worker himself, piecing together clues until he found the right man and placed the full amount back in his hands. The laborer got his daughter's money back, and Moro got nothing but the satisfaction of having gone looking.
